## Job Market Paper

- [Coordination vs. Competition: Local Government Centralization and Metropolitan Growth](https://chasewiedemann.github.io/_site/Projects/WIEDEMANN_MUNI_CENTRALIZATION_2026.pdf)
  + **Abstract**: How does the organization of local government affect population growth? Is growth promoted in centralized governments concentrated in a few large units or decentralized governments consisting of many smaller units? The literature provides conflicting answers to these questions. On one hand, decentralization can promote competition between local governments, providing a market-like mechanism to obtain efficiency in the supply of public goods. On the other, externalities can foster coordination failures that undermine competition. Which of these two opposing forces is more important for local government? In this paper, I use local government employment data from the metropolitan statistical areas of the United States and an IV strategy to estimate the causal effect of local government centralization on growth. I then examine the effect of centralization on local government employment, finances, and the siting decisions of data centers to determine which mechanisms drive the effect on growth. My instrument is derived from a complete history of post offices in the United States and leverages a historical policy change, the implementation of Rural Free Delivery in 1902, to measure the presence of small communities and dispersed populations. I show that the instrument shifts the organization of local government toward decentralization and argue that this shift is plausibly exogenous to the modern outcomes I examine. Using the variation induced by the instrument, I find that centralization causes higher population growth rates, higher total local government employment, more tax revenue to be collected, and fewer data centers to locate in the metropolitan area. Based on these empirical results, I argue that centralized local governments best promote growth, with the most likely mechanism being the resolution of coordination failures.
